name: Adonikam
title: Ancestor of a clan that returned from exile
lifespan: Probably before or during the exile (around the 6th century BC); descendants returned around 538–458 BC
summary: Adonikam was the patriarch of a prominent Jewish family whose descendants returned to Judah from the Babylonian exile. Members of this family are recorded in the lists of returnees both under Zerubbabel's leadership (c. 538 BC) and under Ezra's leadership (c. 458 BC). The name Adonikam means 'my Lord has risen' – a theophoric name testifying to faith in God's restoration. In Ezra 8:13, 'the last' of his descendants who returned home are mentioned, suggesting that the entire family eventually left Babylon to reunite in the promised land. The size of this family group – over 660 people – attests to a significant clan with an important place in the restored Jewish community.

keyEvents.title: Adonikam's descendants return with Zerubbabel
keyEvents.description: 666 of Adonikam's descendants were among those who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel's leadership, following Cyrus's decree that allowed the Jews to go home.

keyEvents.title: Adonikam's family in Nehemiah's list
keyEvents.description: In Nehemiah's register of those who returned from exile, 667 of Adonikam's descendants are listed. The small difference from Ezra's figure of 666 may be due to different times of counting or other factors.

keyEvents.title: The last of Adonikam's clan return with Ezra
keyEvents.description: The last of Adonikam's descendants—Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah—returned with Ezra along with sixty men. The phrase 'the last' suggests that the entire clan had now left Babylon and gathered in Judah.

versions.summary: Adonikam was the head of a family that returned to Judah from the Babylonian exile. His descendants are mentioned among those who returned both with Zerubbabel and with Ezra. The family's name means 'my Lord has risen,' and they were among the faithful Jews who sought to rebuild the community in the promised land.
versions.title: Family Head Who Returned from Exile
versions.reason: [minor] The title is appropriate but could have been more specific by noting that it concerns a patriarch/founder of a clan rather than merely a 'head of household', since Adonikam himself likely lived before the exile and it is his descendants who returned.; [major] The role 'leader' is imprecise. Adonikam is mentioned primarily as a patriarch/clan founder for a family group. There is no biblical text describing him as an active leader. More suitable roles would be 'patriarch' or 'clan founder'.; [minor] The summary states that Adonikam was 'head of a returning family', but it is more precise to say he was the patriarch of a clan that returned. Adonikam himself probably lived long before the return. The name meaning 'my Lord has risen' is correct and well included.; [minor] The fourth and fifth key events ('Registration among the exiles' and 'Part of the rebuilding of the Jewish community') are somewhat generic and overlap with the first three events. They do not add significant new information specifically about Adonikam, and the biblical references are broad contextual texts rather than direct references to Adonikam.; [minor] The number 666 agrees with Ezra 2:13, but it should be noted that Nehemiah 7:18 gives 667. This discrepancy is correctly reflected between the two events, but it could have been useful to comment explicitly on the difference.; [minor] Ezra 8:13 mentions 'the last' of Adonikam's sons. The description is essentially correct, but the phrasing 'the second wave of returnees' is somewhat imprecise – Ezra's group is generally considered a later/third wave after Zerubbabel's and possibly other groups.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. There are several interesting details: the meaning of the name, the discrepancy between 666 (Ezra 2:13) and 667 (Neh 7:18), the unusual phrasing 'the last' in Ezra 8:13, and possible connections to 1 Esdras in the Greek tradition.

versions.summary: Adonikam was the patriarch of a significant Jewish clan whose descendants returned to Judah from the Babylonian exile. The family's descendants are mentioned in the lists of returnees under both Zerubbabel's and Ezra's leadership. The name Adonikam means 'my Lord has risen' – a theophoric name testifying to faith in God's restoration. In Ezra 8:13, 'the last' of his descendants are noted as having returned home, suggesting that the entire clan eventually left Babylon to settle in the Promised Land.
versions.title: Ancestor of a clan that returned from exile
versions.reason: [minor] The lifespan indication "c. 500s BC (descendants)" is somewhat imprecise. Adonikam himself likely lived before the exile or early in the exile period, while his descendants returned around 538–458 BC. It should be clarified that the patriarch himself probably lived earlier than the 500s BC.; [minor] "Founding ancestor" is slightly redundant with "patriarch." The term "clan head" may be a more fitting alternative, reflecting his position within the social structure.; [minor] The final footnote on 1 Esdras/3 Esra could advantageously be categorized as "linguistic" or "other" rather than "historical," since it primarily concerns textual traditions and translation history. Alternatively, it may remain under "historical," but this is a matter of judgment.

footnotes.text: The name Adonikam (Hebrew: אֲדֹנִיקָם) means 'my Lord has risen' or 'the Lord has stood up.' It is a theophoric name expressing faith in God's intervention and restoration – fitting for a clan that returned from exile.

There is a small numerical discrepancy between Ezra 2:13, which lists 666 descendants of Adonikam, and Nehemiah 7:18, which lists 667. Such variations between the lists are common and may result from different counting times, scribal errors, or differing criteria for inclusion.

In Ezra 8:13, the remarkable phrase 'the last' (Hebrew: אַחֲרֹנִים) is used to describe Adonikam's sons who returned with Ezra. This suggests that the entire clan eventually left Babylon and gathered in Judah – a testimony to the family's loyalty to their homeland.

The records in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 served as official genealogical registers confirming Jewish identity and land rights. For families like Adonikam's, such documentation was crucial for participating in the temple rebuilding and religious life in Jerusalem.

In the Greek translation of 1 Esdras (3 Esdras), Adonikam's family is also mentioned, confirming the tradition's widespread acceptance. This text provides a parallel testimony from the Hellenistic Jewish tradition.

Cyrus's decree in 538 BC, which allowed the Jews to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem, is also confirmed by the Cyrus Cylinder – an archaeological find documenting the Persian king's policy of allowing deported peoples to return to their homelands.
